rationale: No panel dissent is in the packet. The judgment changed because the incumbent's per-claim grades violate the anchored-is-not-evidenced rule: five featured claims are held on their anchor alone with no admitted evidence record — the chemistry base-rate mechanism (TRN-C101), the flash-sharpness physics argument (TRN-C102), the geomagnetic decline (TRN-C103), the linear alignments (TRN-C104) and the altitude attribution (TRN-C108) — and the incumbent graded them provisionally or weakly supported. Each is regraded unresolved at low confidence; where admitted records on sibling claims bear on them (TRN-E002 and TRN-E024 for the defect mechanism, TRN-E006 for the sharpness argument, TRN-E017 for the Kp decline, TRN-E018 for alignments, TRN-E025 and TRN-E055 with their context records for the altitude), the reasoning names that basis and says what it does and does not carry. TRN-C122 is regraded from well_supported to provisionally_supported: it rests on one moderate record (TRN-E079), the authors' own three control draws, which is not enough for the higher grade. The case verdict, the load-bearing set, the weakest links and the dossier headers stand; the synthesis keeps TRN-E011 as the record whose removal would most move the case; the steelman is rewritten so the proponents' reading of sharpness is written as their reading. The article keeps the incumbent's structure and plates and is not lengthened in substance: anchor-only claims are now told as what the ledger holds rather than in the page's voice, and a short paragraph sets the fourth account (exotic astrophysics offered on the premise that the flashes are real) beside the other three so the telling matches the accounts field, which is otherwise unchanged; the natural-body account is told once as a family covering storm-aggregated dust and meteoroid debris. Question and accounts are kept. No research item has been settled: TRN-R001 remains open for the blinded outside repeat and the per-generation first-appearance census its own summary says were not performed. Crux order is unchanged; the coma blind test and the flash calibration lead because they are the only tests that reach the flash-versus-flaw crux directly.
article:
On the night of 12 April 1950, the 48-inch Schmidt telescope on Palomar Mountain exposed a red-sensitive glass plate for about fifty minutes — routine work for the first great photographic atlas of the sky. Seventy years later, researchers comparing that plate against everything photographed since found something odd: [nine star-like points, clustered within about ten arcminutes, that appear on that one exposure and on nothing before or since]{claim=TRN-C001}. Not on the overlapping plate taken six days later. Not in modern digital surveys that see several magnitudes deeper. Nine lights, one night, gone.

{plate:IMG-TRN-P01}

The project that found them — VASCO, for Vanishing and Appearing Sources during a Century of Observations, led by astronomer Beatriz Villarroel — has since assembled a working catalog of more than a hundred thousand single-exposure candidates and proposed an explanation with a first-rate pedigree of strangeness: that some of these flashes are sunlight glinting off reflective objects near Earth, photographed years before any nation launched a satellite. That is the version that makes headlines. The interesting dispute lives several rungs below it, and it is worth being precise about what the plates actually show.

## Four accounts of a dot

Every account of the phenomenon must explain the same thing: a small, round, dark grain on a glass negative. Four accounts are on the table; three engage the grain.

**Chemistry.** Photographic emulsion is a chemical medium, and it does not need the sky's permission to make a dot. The skeptical literature holds — pointing to two decades of archival hunts for gamma-ray-burst flashes that ended without a single confirmed transient — that [ordinary emulsion, copying and scanning defects produce isolated, star-like marks on archival plates at rates high enough to contaminate any single-exposure search]{claim=TRN-C101}. This ledger holds that proposition on its anchor: the mechanism is documented as a possibility, and its rate has never been measured. The account predicts that candidates will look like known defects, congregate where defects congregate (plate corners and edges), and that their ensemble patterns will dissolve whenever the catalog is rebuilt from scratch.

**Artificial glints.** The proponents' account holds that [at least some marks are sunlight reflected from objects physically near Earth, at roughly geosynchronous altitudes]{claim=TRN-C021}, and — the headline — that [artificial objects capable of producing them were in orbit before Sputnik 1]{claim=TRN-C022}. Its strong form adds that [the objects were extraterrestrial technological artifacts]{claim=TRN-C023}. It predicts sharp, sub-second images; a deficit of candidates inside Earth's shadow, where a reflector goes dark; groupings and alignments as a tumbling body flashes repeatedly; and signals that sharpen, not fade, as defects are filtered out.

**Natural near-Earth bodies.** A third account accepts that the flashes are real and near Earth but denies the hardware: reflective natural aggregates — icy dust trapped and clumped in the magnetosphere after geomagnetic storms, or meteoroid debris — could glint in the same geometry. It shares the shadow-deficit prediction with the artificial account and parts from it on composition and size.

**Exotic astrophysics.** A fourth, a dark-matter proposal from particle physics, takes the reality of the flashes as its premise and offers no observation bearing on the artifact question; the ledger holds it as context, and it inherits the crux rather than bearing on it.

A reader should keep the first three in view, because most of the evidence below fails to separate the second from the third, and the decisive question sits beneath all of them: was any given mark made by light at all?

## What nobody disputes

Start with what the fiercest critics concede. Hambly — an astronomer at the Royal Observatory Edinburgh and an author of the SuperCOSMOS digitization of the Palomar survey — went to his own institution's plate archive and put the relevant glass under a microscope. The nine marks are there, physically, at the reported positions. They are not scanner glitches or software errors. An [independent detection pipeline, built from scratch by an outside researcher, recovers eight of the nine, three of three from a second event, and about two-thirds of the published 5,399-candidate catalog]{claim=TRN-C004}. And the 1950 event is not alone: [three bright point sources of about 16th magnitude appeared within ten arcseconds of one another on a plate from 19 July 1952 and were gone within about fifty minutes]{claim=TRN-C003}, absent from all later imaging down to magnitude 25.5 — a fade of more than ten magnitudes in under an hour, if it was a fade.

{plate:IMG-TRN-P02}

So the marks are real. The question is what makes a mark.

## The case for chemistry

Hambly and his coauthor Blair supply the conventional account at full strength. Their inspection of the Edinburgh copies found emulsion holes, bubbles and scratch-like marks on both plates, and appear-once detections on the neighbouring field too — the phenomenon recurs wherever one looks. They add two sharper points.

First, a measurement: [the nine 1950 marks are systematically sharper and more concentrated than real star images of the same brightness]{claim=TRN-C002}; all nine fall on the sharp side of the plate's profile distribution, a joint outcome with odds of order one in a billion if they were stars. A classifier trained on confirmed stars, confirmed galaxies and unmatched (likely spurious) detections files the nine with the spurious class — though its spurious class is defined by having no modern counterpart, which is exactly what defines a transient candidate, so a real transient population would be labelled artifact-like by construction.

Second, and more structurally damaging, a genealogy. The two modern digitizations that both show the candidates — the agreement that seemed to rule out simple flaws — [descend from glass copy negatives printed from the same intermediate positive, so a single defect introduced at the shared copying stage would be inherited by both]{claim=TRN-C007}. “It's in two independent datasets” turns out to mean “it's in two cousins.”

{plate:IMG-TRN-P03}

The account is strong and has two unpaid debts. Nobody has measured how often the copying process actually mints star-like fakes, so the mechanism is a possibility argument without a base rate. And its simplest form does not reach evidence gathered outside the Palomar plate family.

## The original glass

The genealogy argument names its own decisive test: only the original negative sits above the shared copying stage. A microscopy study by J. Yang and Beatriz Villarroel — a preprint, not yet peer reviewed — reports the first examination of that material: the glass negative that was inside the Palomar Schmidt on the night of 12 April 1950, held at the Caltech plate archive, registered star by star against the published digitization, together with a Harvard copy plate of the 1952 triple.

It reports that [all nine 1950 sources are present on the original negative at their published positions]{claim=TRN-C024}, and that the 1952 triple appears both on the copy plate and in the original survey digitization. For the two flagship events, “it's in two cousins” is answered with *it's on the grandparent*. The copy-chain mechanism keeps its full force against the hundred thousand uninspected catalog candidates and loses it exactly where the case is fought hardest. The marks are sharp-edged, compact and round where nearby stars are slightly elongated.

And there the good news, for every camp, stops. The study states plainly that microscopy cannot tell a brief flash from a flaw born in the emulsion: at the level of a single source the two produce the same sharp little dot. The microscopist who examined the Caltech plate — directed to the nine objects by Hambly himself — found them un-star-like and concluded that emulsion defects were a reasonable attribution, noting that the field sits in a corner of the plate, where defects are more common. The study prints that opinion against its own interest and argues that it embeds a default: judged only against steady stars, a sub-second flash *is supposed to look* like a defect. Both readings are correct as far as they go. The one clean escape — the same flash caught from a second mountain at the same instant, yielding a parallax distance or nothing — is closed for these events; no simultaneous second-site plate of comparable depth exists.

Two caveats travel with all of this: the examination was not blind, and no one outside the group has repeated the registration. But the shape of the result is clear. “Original or copy?” has an answer for the canonical events: original. “Sky or chemistry?” does not, and per-source microscopy cannot supply it. [Whether any mark was made by light entering the telescope during the original exposure]{claim=TRN-C020} is the crux of the case. It is narrower than it was, and no more settled.

## The case for light

The proponents' reply to the sharpness argument begins with physics. A star sits on the plate for the whole exposure, smeared by atmosphere and imperfect tracking; the proponents argue that [a flash lasting under a second has no time to smear, and should look sharper and rounder than a star]{claim=TRN-C102}. The ledger holds that argument on its anchor — it is a derivation, not a measurement — and if it is right the critics' morphology argument points in either direction, or in none. No one has exposed period-appropriate emulsion to controlled flashes alongside artificial stars and drawn the curve. Until someone does, sharpness is the case's most-cited observation and its least diagnostic one.

The stronger development comes from outside the Palomar archive entirely. Busko, a retired Space Telescope Science Institute developer working independently, searched rapid same-night plate pairs from the Hamburg Observatory — [a different telescope, emulsion stock, archive and digitization, where analogous appear-once candidates with systematically narrow profiles duly show up]{claim=TRN-C010}. Hamburg's plates share no ancestor with Palomar's; the copy-defect mechanism cannot touch them. What the search lacks is a measured candidate rate against matched controls, so “the same phenomenon” and “the same defect susceptibility” remain indistinguishable.

His follow-up goes further. On a telescope chosen for its strong off-axis coma — the little comet-shaped distortion that optics stamp on light arriving away from the axis — [candidate transient images reportedly carry the coma pattern expected for point sources imaged through the optics]{claim=TRN-C011}. Scratches and chemistry do not know where the optical axis is; photons do. If that discriminant survives blind validation against known defects and deliberately produced short flashes, the case changes character: it would be a physical detector of incident light usable across every plate archive on Earth. It has not been blind-validated, it applies only to Hamburg candidates, and the paper itself says the data do not establish the physical origin of the light.

## The statistics, honestly

Above the individual events sits an ensemble argument built on the VASCO working catalog of about 107,875 candidates. Here the record is genuinely, instructively mixed, and the pattern of who reproduces what is the most informative thing in it.

### The shadow

[The catalog shows a deficit of candidates inside Earth's shadow at geosynchronous altitude — roughly 0.46% observed against 1.4% expected]{claim=TRN-C005}. A sunlit reflector at that height goes dark in the shadow; a defect does not care where the shadow is. This is the best geometric evidence the two near-Earth accounts have, and they share it.

An independent statistician reanalysing the same catalog with his own code reproduces the deficit. A machine-learning study that scores each candidate for artifact likelihood finds [the deficit grows stronger, at every assumed altitude, once defect-like rows are filtered out]{claim=TRN-C129}. A modelling preprint fits the deficit's dependence on angle from the antisolar point to spherical shells and infers [a characteristic altitude of roughly 20,000–35,000 km]{claim=TRN-C108}, with the deficit largest at 25,000 km on the full catalog — a range its authors describe as a spread across samples and estimators rather than a confidence interval, from a model that fits poorly in absolute terms and omits orbital motion.

Against this, the most comprehensive critique — by Watters and colleagues, several of whom work in UAP-research organizations and take anomaly claims seriously — shows that the uniform background the shadow analysis assumes is false: candidates rise toward plate corners and edges and gather in geometric clusters and voids. Under a proper null there is no significant deficit in their closely related datasets, and at least 91% of the rows used in the ensemble studies belong to a set earlier removed for lying within 5 arcseconds of catalogued stars. The proponents reply that the critics' subset is twenty times smaller, built for another purpose, and underpowered. The modelling preprint quietly concedes part of the point: it restricts its analysis to a sky region chosen to avoid empty stripes and edge effects that “may influence the results.” The deficit's magnitude, meanwhile, changes with the formula, the assumed altitude and the cut applied, and the filter that strengthens it is the group's own classifier, trained on the group's own visual labels; a classifier that removes defect-like rows would sharpen any signal that defects dilute, whether or not what remains is the sky.

### The bombs

[Candidate rates are elevated within a day of atmospheric nuclear tests, with a relative risk of about 1.45]{claim=TRN-C006}. This reproduces on the original rows with independent code, survives weather and moonlight controls and a permutation test, survives an open Bayesian reanalysis that models temporal autocorrelation (attenuated, and with a lag term for UAP reports now stronger than the nuclear one), and strengthens among candidates the ML model scores as likelier real. A separate preprint reports — a result this ledger holds on its anchor, with no evidence record yet admitted — that [candidate rates decline with geomagnetic activity, and that controlling for it strengthens the nuclear association]{claim=TRN-C103}; a companion test finds that plate sensitivity itself — star counts, limiting magnitude — does not vary with storms, closing one environmental route to a spurious pattern. Both rest on the same catalog.

But the one fully independent reconstruction — Hayes's pipeline, which rebuilt a candidate catalog from whole-plate scans rather than accepting anyone's rows — finds no significant nuclear effect once nightly sky coverage is modelled: a relative risk of 1.35 with a confidence interval spanning 1, and an incidence ratio of 1.03 in the exposure-weighted model. Watters traces the timing largely to the observing schedule. And the hotspot preprint discussed below reports — on the paper's word alone; no evidence record yet — that [all 203 high-probability transients recorded the night before the Castle Yankee test project onto Pacific regions west of Mexico and Central America]{claim=TRN-C125}, which is to say the high-confidence nuclear-window sample is dominated by a single night's plates, a fact that turns a correlation over a hundred thousand rows into a question about a handful of physical plates nobody has inspected.

The pattern is the tell: the correlations reproduce *conditional on the working catalog* and dissolve when the catalog is rebuilt. That does not prove they are artifacts. It proves the catalog is the battleground. Note too what the nuclear correlation could not establish even if it survived: fallout settling on plates predicts it as well as glinting objects do.

### The hotspots

The newest proponent result projects each high-probability candidate along its line of sight from Palomar to a shell at 35,786 km and asks which patch of Earth it hangs over. [Sixteen of 137 Earth-fixed cells show an excess over the group's own random control that survives Bonferroni correction]{claim=TRN-C119}, concentrated over the eastern Pacific west of southern Mexico, the southern Gulf of Mexico, and one cell in the southwestern United States. [Fourteen of the sixteen draw their excess from at least two plates]{claim=TRN-C132}; [two adjacent cells draw theirs from a single plate, XE435]{claim=TRN-C133}. The preprint reads the geography against locations from UAP lore and, to its credit, calls the intelligence interpretation “unfortunately not falsifiable.”

Three things limit it. Every projected location depends on the assumed altitude — at the 20,000 km the companion paper's own estimator prefers, the same candidates hang over different cells. The excess is measured against the same working catalog and ML filter as every other group result, so a plate with a high defect rate projects its excess to whatever cell the geometry assigns it; hotspot significance is not a test of the sky, and the paper concedes that agreement between its two methods “does not rule out this possibility.” And its own negative control undercuts its clustering method: [random plate-aware positions, clustered by the same procedure, meet or exceed the silhouette threshold the authors adopt as indicating non-random clustering]{claim=TRN-C122}. Only three control draws were run. A related line reports — held here on its anchor, the paper not read in full for this ledger — that [some multiple-transient events form linear alignments]{claim=TRN-C104}; a second preprint finds alignments exceeding Monte Carlo expectations on seven plates, a pattern that inherits every provenance problem of the marks it is drawn on, found with an alignment criterion chosen after the fact.

## Which near-Earth?

Suppose the near-Earth geometry survived. Which of the two near-Earth accounts would it favour? The modelling preprint argues that [millimetre-scale dusty-plasma grains cannot produce the centimetre-to-metre reflecting facets its own brightness model infers]{claim=TRN-C117}. But that inference rests on assumed altitude, specularity, flash duration and reflectivity, and on a catalog from which bright sources were excluded by construction — which the authors concede biases the inferred sizes downward. One toy model excluding another does not move the observation rung. The same preprint finds [no robust association between candidate dates and annual meteor showers]{claim=TRN-C116}, closing one natural pathway (cometary debris) while leaving a persistent natural population untested.

The preprint then argues that [among the toy models it considers — natural bodies, dusty plasma, non-human intelligence — only the last accommodates all five reported features: sharp profiles, groupings, the shadow deficit, the nuclear timing and the geomagnetic anticorrelation]{claim=TRN-C118}. This is an argument from residual fit among a hand-chosen set, premised on three features contested at the catalog level and one that both camps read their own way. It is not a test, and the authors add that nature can always surprise us. Nothing in the record bears on the extraterrestrial branch at all; even a proven pre-Sputnik object would need a separate origin argument before that word earned its place.

## The ladder, and where it breaks

Climb the ladder and watch the support thin. That the marks exist on plate material: settled, by the critics themselves. That the canonical nine are on the original negative: reported, pending review. That the marks are reproducible by independent software: settled. That the population statistics mean anything: contested at the level of dataset definition — at present they survive only in the catalog they were found in. That any mark was made by light entering the telescope: unresolved, the crux, with every rung above it conditional. That the light came from near Earth: unresolved, resting on a contested shadow geometry that two different accounts share. That artificial objects orbited before Sputnik: the headline claim, unresolved. That they were extraterrestrial: not presently testable, by the proponents' own account.

## What would change our mind

Toward light: a blind validation of the coma discriminant that separates deliberately produced flashes from the full defect bestiary; a flash-profile calibration on period emulsion showing the nine marks match sub-second flashes and not defects; a shadow deficit that appears in an independently extracted catalog under a preregistered null that models the plate background as it actually is.

Toward chemistry: a measured census of copy-stage and emulsion defects showing star-like marks at the rates the ensemble needs; the Castle Yankee-night plates showing their 203 candidates concentrated on one or two plates with edge clustering and defect morphology; the coma discriminant failing its blind test; independent-observatory candidate rates that match matched-control defect rates.

Toward one near-Earth account over the other: an altitude estimate that survives independent shadow code and orbital dynamics, and a size inference that does not depend on excluding the brightest candidates.

Per-source microscopy is exhausted. What remains discriminating is the coma signature, ensemble statistics on catalogs nobody's thumb has touched, and — for any future event — simultaneous imaging from two or more stations, which turns a single ambiguous dot into a measured distance or a local artifact. The research agenda, ranked by how much each test would move the case, follows.

assessment.synthesis: The case is bottom-heavy. The observation rung is as secure as photographic evidence permits: the nine 1950 marks are physical emulsion features confirmed by the critics on the Edinburgh copy (TRN-E002), recovered by an independent pipeline (TRN-E008), and reported present on the original Caltech glass (TRN-E022), which removes the copy-chain route (TRN-C007, TRN-E005) as an explanation for the two flagship events (TRN-E023). It does not settle the crux: TRN-C020 has narrowed from original-or-copy to flash-or-flaw in the original emulsion, and the microscopy authors concede their method cannot decide that, with their own microscopist leaning defect (TRN-E024). Sharpness (TRN-C002) is a credible measurement of indeterminate direction — TRN-E003, TRN-E004 and TRN-E006 read it three ways with no calibration — and the physics argument that flashes should be sharp (TRN-C102) is held on its anchor alone, as is the chemistry account's claim that defects arise at contaminating rates (TRN-C101): the two mechanisms that would decide the crux are both unmeasured. The ensemble claims split cleanly by replication type: they survive reanalysis of the author-supplied rows (TRN-E010, TRN-E015, TRN-E019, TRN-E025, TRN-E052) and fail independent extraction and a corrected null (TRN-E009, TRN-E011); the modelling preprint concedes part of the background objection (TRN-E051) and the hotspot preprint's own negative control meets its non-randomness criterion (TRN-E079). This pattern indicts the catalog, not yet the sky. The attribution rung inherits all of it: TRN-E074 assumes rather than tests near-Earth origin; TRN-E020's natural-aggregate route means even a vindicated geometry would not select the artificial branch, and TRN-E038 excludes it only through a selection-biased size model (TRN-E062, TRN-E063); the proponents call the intelligence reading unfalsifiable (TRN-E083). Sensitivity: the single record whose removal would most change the case is TRN-E011 — the only strong record against the shadow deficit; without it TRN-C005 rises to provisionally supported and TRN-C021 with it, moving the near-Earth version of the hypothesis toward weakly supported while leaving TRN-C020 untouched. Runner-up is TRN-E022, whose removal collapses TRN-C024 and restores the copy-chain hypothesis's reach over the canonical events. The case verdict survives the removal of either.
assessment.steelman: Nine sharp, round marks lie within ten arcminutes of one another on one fifty-minute exposure, on the original telescope negative (TRN-E022), and not on the overlapping plate taken six days later (TRN-E002); a second event puts three sixteenth-magnitude points within ten arcseconds that vanish within the hour and never return to magnitude 25.5 — a ten-magnitude drop — and the most isolated of the three has a profile indistinguishable from a star (TRN-E007). The proponents read the nine marks' sharpness as exactly what a sub-second flash should leave on a long exposure (TRN-E006), and the defect account has no measured base rate for spatially clustered, star-like flaws on original negatives (TRN-R007 unfilled; TRN-C101 anchor-only). The defect account must also explain why the ensemble signals strengthen rather than weaken under a classifier trained to remove defects (TRN-E015, TRN-E052, TRN-E053), why plate sensitivity is invariant to the geomagnetic activity the candidate rate is reported to track (TRN-E017), and why an independent archive with no shared ancestry shows candidates with narrow profiles and, on the author's reading, the coma signature of light through the optics (TRN-E013, TRN-E014). No single defect mechanism in the ledger accounts for clustering, sharpness, filter-strengthening and cross-archive recurrence together. This assessment does not answer that conjunction; it holds that each element is individually undercut (unblinded, uncalibrated, same-catalog, unvalidated) and that a conjunction of undercut elements is not yet evidence.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least some single-exposure, star-like detections on pre-Sputnik photographic plates are genuine optical flashes recorded through the telescope — and, on the strong version of the hypothesis, sunlight reflections from artificial objects near Earth before October 1957, with an extraterrestrial origin proposed as the only toy model fitting all reported features.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether the marks exist — critics physically confirmed the canonical nine on copy glass and the proponents report them on the original negative — but one rung up: whether any mark was made by light entering the telescope rather than by a flaw in the emulsion (microscopy cannot tell, by the proponents' own account, and neither the defect base rate nor the flash-profile physics has been measured); whether any ensemble signal (Earth-shadow deficit, nuclear-test timing, Earth-projected hotspots) survives independent catalog construction and a non-uniform background null rather than merely independent re-analysis of the same contested rows; and, if the near-Earth geometry held, whether anything distinguishes artificial reflectors from natural ones.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: Blind-validate a physical incident-light discriminant (the coma-aberration signature) against known defects and deliberately produced flashes, and calibrate flash profiles on period emulsion, so that individual marks can be classified as light or flaw; then reproduce the Earth-shadow deficit, or another orbital signature, in an independently extracted candidate population under a preregistered null that models the plate background as observed. The first would establish real flashes; the second would begin to establish a near-Earth reflective population. Artificiality would need an independent size or structure argument not built on a bright-source-excluded catalog; extraterrestrial origin has no test on the table.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Photographic archives manufacture star-like marks without any sky event: emulsion flaws, development chemistry, handling damage and — for POSS-I specifically — defects introduced on the shared intermediate positive from which both major digitizations descend, so that a single copying flaw appears 'independently' in two modern datasets. The critics' own inspection found emulsion holes, bubbles and scratch-like marks on the copy plates and appear-once detections on the neighbouring field; the microscopist who examined the original 1950 negative judged emulsion defects a reasonable attribution and noted the field lies in a plate corner where defects congregate. The ensemble correlations, on this account, are properties of an unvalidated working catalog — 91% of whose rows were earlier flagged as lying within 5 arcseconds of catalogued stars — together with the Palomar observing schedule and a plate background that rises toward corners and edges; they reproduce when the rows are reused and vanish when the catalog is rebuilt. Hotspot and clustering results project per-plate defect rates onto whatever Earth cell a fixed-altitude geometry assigns them, and the paper's own random controls meet its clustering criterion. The account's unpaid debts: no measured base rate for star-like defects per copying stage or on original emulsion (the rate claim is held on its anchor alone), and no reach over an independent archive whose candidates reportedly carry the optical signature of light through the telescope.

components.label: Marks exist on surviving plate material and are software-independent

components.note: TRN-E024 caps microscopy; TRN-E014 is unvalidated; TRN-E004/E011 undermine; both deciding mechanisms (TRN-C101, TRN-C102) are anchor-only.

components.note: Rests on the contested shadow deficit; TRN-E074 assumes it; altitude fits (TRN-E025, E055) are poor-fit, not confidence intervals; natural and artificial accounts share the geometry (TRN-E020).

components.label: Artificial and extraterrestrial attribution
components.note: TRN-C022 unresolved on two weak qualifying records; TRN-C023 declared unfalsifiable by its proponents (TRN-E083); TRN-E038/E072 are toy-model arguments.

researchPriority.reason: Several desk-tier tests (TRN-R004, TRN-R008, TRN-R005) could decide the ensemble rung in either direction on existing scans, and two lab-tier tests (TRN-R003, TRN-R002) reach the flash-versus-flaw crux that no evidence record currently touches; the case has unusually many cheap, decisive, unrun experiments.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Two weak qualifying records only (TRN-E018 alignments on the same contested catalog; TRN-E020, which proposes a natural near-Earth population that would satisfy the same geometry). The claim depends on TRN-C020 and TRN-C021, both unresolved; no record in the ledger separates artificial from natural reflectors, and the only size argument (TRN-E038) rests on a selection-biased model (TRN-E062, TRN-E063).

treatment.plainLanguage: Human-made or otherwise artificial reflective objects were orbiting Earth before the first satellite and caused the flashes.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis; if established it decides the case. Nothing in the ledger presently tests it independently of the rungs below.
treatment.strongestObjection: Even granting real near-Earth glints, storm-aggregated icy dust or debris (TRN-E020) predicts the shadow geometry equally well, and the facet-size inference that would exclude it is a floor set by excluding bright sources.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blind-validated incident-light discriminant applied to Palomar candidates
A shadow deficit reproduced on an independently extracted catalog under a preregistered non-uniform-background null (TRN-R005)
A size or structure argument for the reflectors that does not depend on the bright-source-excluded catalog

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E083 records the proponents' own statement that the intelligence interpretation is not falsifiable; TRN-E084 is context. TRN-E072's toy-model argument was judged at intake to bear on TRN-C118, not on this claim. No record offers a test.

treatment.plainLanguage: The objects were made by a non-human intelligence.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: No observation in the ledger, or proposed in the research agenda, distinguishes this from any other origin of a pre-Sputnik object; it cannot presently decide anything.
treatment.strongestObjection: Its own proponents call it unfalsifiable; even a proven pre-Sputnik artifact would need a separate origin argument.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A proposed observation that would come out differently under a non-human origin than under a human or natural one
Physical recovery or resolved imaging of one of the objects

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E074 (weak, supports) infers a one-third solar-reflection fraction from the shadow deficit while explicitly assuming real orbital sources; TRN-E020 (weak, qualifies) and TRN-E021 (context) take the reality of the flashes as premise. The claim stands or falls with TRN-C005, which is mixed, and with TRN-C020, which is unresolved.

treatment.plainLanguage: At least some flashes are sunlight bouncing off something near Earth, not light from deep space.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Would separate the two near-Earth accounts from both chemistry and the exotic-astrophysics account, but not from each other.
treatment.strongestObjection: The only geometric evidence is the shadow deficit, which disappears under the critics' corrected null (TRN-E011) and has been shown only on the group's own rows.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An altitude-dependent shadow signature on Hayes's independent catalog with independent shadow code (TRN-R012)
A parallax distance from simultaneous two-station imaging of a future event (TRN-R009)
A null on the independent catalog, which would remove the geometric argument

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supporting: TRN-E014 (moderate; coma pattern on Hamburg candidates, unvalidated, not Palomar). Undermining: TRN-E004 (moderate; classifier groups the nine with artifacts), TRN-E011 (strong; no feature shown to be an optical transient). Qualifying: TRN-E006 (sharpness cuts both ways), TRN-E024 (microscopy cannot separate flash from emulsion flaw; the microscopist leaned defect). TRN-E021 is context. The deciding mechanisms on each side (TRN-C101, TRN-C102) are anchor-only. The verdict is the finding: the crux has narrowed to flash-or-flaw and no admitted record can decide it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of these dots were made by light coming through the telescope during the exposure, not by a flaw in the glass, the copy, or the scan.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every rung above depends on it; if false, the whole case is plate chemistry.
treatment.strongestObjection: The only person to inspect the original negative attributed the nine marks to emulsion defects in a plate corner, and the critics' morphology classifier agrees.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blind validation of the coma discriminant on a corpus including deliberate flashes and the full defect bestiary (TRN-R003)
A flash-profile calibration on period emulsion placing the nine marks with flashes or with defects (TRN-R002)
A measured defect census showing clustered star-like flaws at the needed rate on original negatives (TRN-R007)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E005 (strong) documents the contact-printing genealogy from Hambly's own knowledge of the archive. TRN-E023 (moderate, qualifies) does not dispute the genealogy but removes its reach over the two canonical events, which TRN-E022 places on the original negative.

treatment.plainLanguage: The two modern scans that both show the dots were printed from the same intermediate copy, so a flaw in that copy would appear in both.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes a pathway, not an occurrence; it dissolves the two-datasets argument for the uninspected catalog but no longer bears on the flagship events.
treatment.strongestObjection: For the nine 1950 marks the copy-stage route is closed by their presence on the original, and no base rate exists for copy-stage star-like defects.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A per-generation first-appearance census across surviving positives and copy negatives (TRN-R007)
An outside blinded repeat of the Caltech registration (TRN-R001)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E001 (discovery), TRN-E002 (strong; critics' physical confirmation on the Edinburgh copy), TRN-E008 (strong; eight of nine recovered independently), TRN-E022 (present on the original). Uncontested by any record.

treatment.plainLanguage: Nine star-like dots really are on the plate from 12 April 1950 and are missing from the plate six days later and from every modern survey.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Common ground: the existence of the marks does not separate flash from defect.
treatment.strongestObjection: The same inspection found appear-once detections on the neighbouring plate and visible blemishes on both, so recurrence is what defects also produce.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Nothing plausible; the observation rung is settled by the critics themselves

claimAssessments.reasoning: One moderate record (TRN-E022): registration of the Caltech original against the digitization finds all nine at their positions. Unreviewed, not blinded, performed by the proponents' group, though the microscopist was directed to the objects by Hambly. No contradicting record.

treatment.plainLanguage: The nine dots are on the actual glass that was in the telescope, not only on later copies.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Closes the copy-chain route for the nine; leaves the emulsion-flaw route fully open, as TRN-E024 states.
treatment.strongestObjection: The registration is the load-bearing step and no one outside the group has checked it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent, blinded registration of the Caltech plate (TRN-R001)
Publication with figures allowing outside verification

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E003 (strong) reports the measurement; TRN-E004 and TRN-E006 dispute only its interpretation. The measurement is common ground.

treatment.plainLanguage: The nine dots are tighter and rounder than stars of the same brightness on the same plate.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Read as a defect signature by TRN-E004 and as a flash signature by TRN-E006; without the calibration of TRN-R002 its direction is unknown.
treatment.strongestObjection: Both a sub-second flash and an emulsion defect are expected to look sharper than a star, so the observation may discriminate nothing.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A flash-profile calibration on period emulsion showing the two distributions separate and where the nine fall (TRN-R002)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E007 (moderate; discovery with deep follow-up), TRN-E008 (strong; three of three recovered independently), TRN-E022 (present on copy plate and original digitization). TRN-E018 qualifies weakly by extending the alignment line.

treatment.plainLanguage: Three bright dots appeared close together on a July 1952 plate and were gone from the next exposure less than an hour later, and from everything since.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A ten-magnitude fade within the hour is hard for any astrophysical source; the star-like profile of the isolated member is a puzzle for both defect and flash accounts.
treatment.strongestObjection: No physical inspection of the 1952 original has been published; presence on the original is inferred from the digitization.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Microscopy of the 1952 original negative
A defect census showing clustered bright star-like flaws at measurable rates

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E008 (strong): from-scratch pipeline recovers the canonical events and 63.9% of the 5,399 catalog. TRN-E016 supplies the catalog-construction context.

treatment.plainLanguage: An outsider's software finds the same dots without using the team's code or lists.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Shows the marks are software-independent, not that they are real; the same pipeline's 2.85-million-candidate sweep shows how far the population depends on vetting choices.
treatment.strongestObjection: Independent extraction, not independent material — it reads the same digitized copies.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Failure to recover the canonical events under calibrated parameters

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supporting on the author-supplied rows: TRN-E010 (moderate), TRN-E015 (moderate, own classifier), TRN-E017 (moderate; closes one confounder). Undermining: TRN-E011 (strong; background non-uniform, no deficit under proper null). Qualifying: TRN-E012 (weak rebuttal), TRN-E051 (the group's own concession that stripes and edges may influence results). TRN-E016 context. The deficit reproduces on the same rows and has not been shown on any other.

treatment.plainLanguage: Fewer candidates appear where Earth's shadow would fall on an object at satellite height.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If real on an independent catalog under a proper null, it would be the best geometric evidence for near-Earth reflectors; as it stands, it is a property of one catalog.
treatment.strongestObjection: The uniform-background assumption is false, and under the corrected null the deficit is not significant.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered shadow analysis across independently constructed catalogs (TRN-R005)
A null result on Hayes's independent catalog (TRN-R012)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E052 and TRN-E053 (moderate, supports) report the strengthening at all tested altitudes and its peak at 35,000 km on the quality-filtered sample. Both come from the same preprint, use the group's own classifier, and reach a small-number regime (17 in shadow at ≥35,000 km).

treatment.plainLanguage: When the team's artifact filter removes defect-like candidates, the shadow gap gets bigger.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A filter trained to remove defect-like rows sharpens any signal defects dilute, whether or not the remainder is the sky; not independent of TRN-E015.
treatment.strongestObjection: The filter's labels are the group's own visual judgments about the same imagery under dispute.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The same strengthening under an independently trained classifier on an independently extracted catalog

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record of its own. Records on its dependency claims bear on it: TRN-E025 (deficit largest at 25,000 km) and TRN-E055 (χ² minimum at 20,000 km), with TRN-E054, TRN-E056 and TRN-E057 recording that the fit has reduced χ² of 3.5–5.4, omits orbital dynamics, and that the range is not a confidence interval. That basis supports only that the group's estimator prefers 20,000–35,000 km; it does not establish that a population responsible for the deficit exists there, which is conditional on TRN-C005 and TRN-C021.

treatment.plainLanguage: The reflecting objects are said to sit roughly 20,000 to 35,000 km up.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An altitude that survived independent code and dynamics would discriminate near-Earth from defect and fix the projection the hotspot results depend on; the present estimate cannot.
treatment.strongestObjection: A poorly fitting toy model on contested rows, whose preferred altitude differs from the one the companion hotspot paper assumes.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered shell fit with orbital dynamics and independent shadow code on three catalogs returning overlapping intervals (TRN-R012)

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supporting on the same rows: TRN-E010 (moderate; RR 1.45, controls, permutation), TRN-E015 (moderate; strengthens under ML filter), TRN-E017 (moderate; sensitivity invariant to Kp). Undermining: TRN-E009 (strong; independent extraction with exposure modelling gives IRR 1.03), TRN-E011 (strong; schedule-driven). Qualifying: TRN-E019 (attenuated; UAP lag stronger), TRN-E012. TRN-E016 context. Reproduces on the catalog, fails when the catalog is rebuilt.

treatment.plainLanguage: More candidates appear on nights within a day of atmospheric nuclear tests.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if real, fallout on plates predicts it as well as glinting objects; and the high-confidence sample is reported to be dominated by one night (TRN-C125, anchor-only).
treatment.strongestObjection: The only independent reconstruction finds no effect once nightly coverage is modelled.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered exposure-denominator analysis on plate logs (TRN-R008)
A plate-level audit of the Castle Yankee night (TRN-R010)

claimAssessments.reasoning: One moderate record (TRN-E013): preliminary sample of 41 Hamburg plate pairs with analogous narrow-profile appear-once candidates; no false-positive calibration or matched-control rate.

treatment.plainLanguage: The same kind of one-night-only dots turn up on plates from a different observatory with no shared copying history.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Escapes the copy-chain mechanism entirely, but cannot yet distinguish a shared sky phenomenon from a shared emulsion failure mode.
treatment.strongestObjection: Old emulsions may fail similarly everywhere; without a rate against controls, recurrence is expected under chemistry too.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A measured candidate rate versus matched controls with injection-recovery completeness (TRN-R006)

claimAssessments.reasoning: One moderate record (TRN-E014): coma pattern reported on Hamburg candidates from a telescope chosen for strong off-axis coma; single author, not blind-validated, defect classes mimicking directional asymmetry not excluded; the paper says the data do not establish the light's physical origin.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some candidate images show the tell-tale comet-shaped smear that the telescope's optics stamp on real light arriving off-centre.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If validated, a physical detector of light through the optics usable on any archive — the only discriminant on the table that reaches the crux.
treatment.strongestObjection: Unblinded, single-author, and some defect classes could imitate directional asymmetry.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blind validation with a frozen classifier against deliberate flashes and the full defect bestiary (TRN-R003)
Application of a validated discriminant to Palomar candidates

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor (Watters' review of GRB-era searches) with no admitted evidence record; a source is not evidence. Records on other claims bear on the mechanism without measuring its rate: TRN-E002 records blemishes and appear-once detections on both copy plates, TRN-E024 records a microscopist attributing the nine to emulsion defects, and TRN-E008 shows an extraction can yield millions of single-exposure detections. None quantifies how often defects produce isolated star-like marks, which is the claim's content.

treatment.plainLanguage: Flaws in the emulsion, copying and scanning make star-like dots often enough to fill a one-night-only search with fakes.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The chemistry account's load-bearing rung: a measured high base rate would undercut every single-exposure candidate; a low one would make clustered sharp marks anomalous.
treatment.strongestObjection: Decades of archival flash-hunting and the critics' own inspection show the impostors exist; the debt is the number, not the mechanism.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A census of star-like defects per copying generation and on original emulsion (TRN-R007)
Independent-archive candidate rates matching matched-control defect rates (TRN-R006)

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record of its own. TRN-E006, admitted on TRN-C002 and TRN-C020, states the same argument and is itself a derivation, not a measurement; the two profile distributions may overlap entirely. No calibration exists.

treatment.plainLanguage: A split-second flash should leave a tighter, rounder dot than a star that sat on the plate for fifty minutes.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true and calibrated, it would neutralize the critics' reading of sharpness and could turn the shared measurement into a flash signature; it cannot by itself prove any flash.
treatment.strongestObjection: Defects also look sharper than stars, so the prediction may not discriminate.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Controlled flash exposures on period emulsion alongside artificial stars (TRN-R002)

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record. TRN-E017, admitted on TRN-C006 and TRN-C005, bears on it by showing plate sensitivity does not vary with Kp, which rules out one artifact route for a decline but does not establish the decline itself. Same 107,875-row lineage as the contested ensemble claims.

treatment.plainLanguage: Fewer candidates appear when Earth's magnetic field is stormy, and accounting for that makes the nuclear-test link look stronger.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A defect population has no obvious reason to track space weather, so a robust decline would favour a real near-Earth population — natural or artificial alike — but it inherits the catalog.
treatment.strongestObjection: Unmeasured in this ledger, and the catalog it runs on has not survived independent extraction for its other correlations.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Kp decline reproduced on Hayes's independent catalog with the exposure denominator of TRN-R008

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor; the source paper was not read in full for the ledger and no evidence record is admitted on it. TRN-E018 (weak, qualifies; admitted on TRN-C003 and TRN-C022) reports alignments on seven plates with a post-hoc criterion and modest p-values, inheriting the catalog's provenance.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some groups of one-night dots line up as if along a path across the sky.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Alignments are what a moving or tumbling reflector predicts and defects do not, but the criterion was chosen after the fact and the marks' origin is unresolved.
treatment.strongestObjection: Alignment searches over many plates are the classic setting for look-elsewhere inflation; a third of reported linear-cluster features were not confidently distinguished from catalogued stars (TRN-E011).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered alignment criterion applied to an independently extracted catalog with full trials accounting

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E041 (moderate, supports) reports the 16-of-137 excess; TRN-E078 (context) records the fixed-altitude projection. The excess is relative to the group's own control on the same catalog and filter; data are not public.

treatment.plainLanguage: Traced down to Earth at satellite height, the candidates pile up over certain patches more than random points do.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A plate with a high defect rate projects its excess to whichever cell the geometry assigns; hotspot significance is not a test of the sky, as the paper concedes.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every location moves with the assumed altitude, and the companion paper's own estimator prefers a different one.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The same regions recurring across altitudes, grids and Hayes's independent catalog (TRN-R011)

claimAssessments.reasoning: One moderate record (TRN-E079): the paper's first random control reaches silhouette 0.50, its own threshold for non-random clustering. Only three control draws; no null distribution given. Uncontested, but a single record from the paper under review.

treatment.plainLanguage: Random points, run through the same clustering method, also pass the test the authors use to call clustering non-random.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A negative control that works against the proponents: it removes the clustering criterion's discriminating power, leaving the excess analysis to carry the hotspot result alone.
treatment.strongestObjection: Three draws cannot establish a null distribution; the real sample's 0.70 may still lie outside it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A null distribution of silhouette values from at least a thousand control draws (TRN-R011)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E038 (weak, supports) states the size mismatch; it rests on the facet-size inference of TRN-C111, whose own records (TRN-E062, TRN-E063) concede that excluding bright sources biases sizes downward and whose inputs are all assumed (TRN-E060).

treatment.plainLanguage: Clumps of millimetre-sized dust are too small to make flashes this bright, so the icy-dust idea is out — if the size estimates hold.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: One toy model excluding another, both premised on real flashes; it does not move the observation rung and is only as good as a selection-biased size model.
treatment.strongestObjection: The size inference is a floor set by catalog selection, and the dusty-plasma mechanism was not modelled directly.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A size inference including bright candidates and measured flash durations
Direct modelling of aggregate reflectivity under the storm-trapping mechanism

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E072 (weak, supports) restates the authors' toy-model comparison; TRN-E073 (weak, qualifies) records their caveat that nature can surprise. Three of the five features are contested at the catalog level (TRN-C005, TRN-C006, TRN-C103) and one is read both ways (TRN-C002).

treatment.plainLanguage: Of the explanations the team tried, only a non-human intelligence fits all five patterns they report.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An argument from residual fit among a hand-chosen set; it is not a test and its premises are unresolved.
treatment.strongestObjection: The set of models is the authors' own and the features it fits have not survived independent catalog construction.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Any of the five features failing on an independent catalog, which would dissolve the premise
A natural model shown to accommodate the same features
